name: ADRs / design docs
description: Write down the why, not just the what — future me is the main audience. Lightweight ADRs beat tribal memory.

name: Continuous delivery
description: Small, always-releasable changes through an automated pipeline. Deploys should be boring, frequent and reversible.

name: Feature flags
description: Decouple deploy from release and make rollback a config change. Adopt for anything risky or user-facing.

name: Infrastructure as Code
description: Non-negotiable for anything beyond a scratch environment: reviewed, versioned, reproducible infrastructure. Manual console changes are how you get drift and outages.

name: Monorepo
description:
Default for related projects: atomic changes, shared tooling, one CI.

Adopt when the projects genuinely change together; split when they don't.

name: Observability
description: Emit structured events, traces and metrics from day one. Debugging anything on-call without them is guesswork.

name: Pair programming
description: The best tool I know for spreading knowledge and catching mistakes early. Adopt for tricky or high-risk work — not all day, every day.

name: Docker
description:
Default way to package and run anything, dev and prod. The image is the unit of deployment.

Avoid only where a serverless deploy or a single compiled binary is genuinely simpler.

name: GitHub Actions
description:
CI/CD that lives next to the code, with a huge marketplace of actions and no extra infrastructure to run.

Good enough for almost everything; self-hosted runners only once I hit its limits.

name: OpenTelemetry
description: Default instrumentation format for traces, metrics and logs — vendor-neutral, so I'm not locked to one backend. Instrument once, ship wherever.

name: PostgreSQL
description:
Default database, full stop. JSONB, extensions and a real query planner mean I rarely need a second datastore.

Reach past it only for genuinely specialised needs — search, extreme write scale, embeddings.

name: Redis
description:
Default cache, lightweight queue and ephemeral state store. Cheap to run and hard to misuse.

Not a primary source of truth.

name: Ruff
description: Replaces flake8, isort and Black with one fast tool and sane defaults. No reason to keep the old chain.

name: Terraform / OpenTofu
description:
Default for provisioning cloud infrastructure: declarative, reviewable and state-tracked. OpenTofu is the hedge if licensing becomes a problem.

I'd avoid it for dynamic, high-churn resources better managed from the application or from Kubernetes manifests.

name: uv
description: Fast, single tool for virtualenvs, dependencies and Python versions. It has made the old pip/virtualenv/pyenv dance obsolete for me.

name: Vite
description:
Default frontend build and dev server: fast HMR, minimal config, works across most stacks.

Step down to a framework's own tooling only if it conflicts.

name: AWS
description:
Default cloud. I know it, it has everything, and the boring services — S3, RDS, SQS, Lambda — are reliable.

Cost and complexity are the price.

name: AWS Lambda / serverless
description:
Default for small, event-driven and bursty workloads: no servers, pay per use, scales to zero.

Avoid for long-running, latency-sensitive or stateful work.

name: Docker Compose
description: Default way to run a multi-service stack locally. If something can't run under Compose, that's usually a smell worth fixing.

name: GitHub
description: Default home for code, review, issues and CI. Network effects make it the obvious choice.

name: Linux
description: Everything I deploy runs here, and with containers and Nix it's a workable dev target too.

name: Nix / NixOS
description:
Reproducible, declarative environments for dev and servers — the real answer to "works on my machine".

The steep learning curve is the cost, so adopt with eyes open.

name: Node.js
description:
Default runtime for TypeScript/JavaScript work, server and CLI alike. One language across the stack is the main draw.

I'd move to Go when I need predictable throughput or a small container image.

name: Python
description:
Default language for almost everything I build: services, scripts, data work and glue. The ecosystem and the fact that most people can read it beat any performance argument for the kind of work I do.

I'd reach for something else only when I need real concurrency or a single static binary.

name: React
description:
Still my default view layer: the component model, ecosystem and my familiarity make me productive immediately.

I'd avoid it for essentially static pages where plain HTML or a server-rendered template carries far less machinery.

name: Tailwind CSS
description:
Utility CSS removes the naming-and-abstraction tax and lets me build consistent UI quickly.

Fine to skip if the team already has a strong component library or design-token system.

name: TypeScript
description:
Default for anything with a UI or a browser in the loop. Types catch the class of bug I actually hit, and the tooling is the best in class.

Not worth the ceremony for throwaway scripts.

name: Prometheus + Grafana
description:
The standard metrics, alerting and dashboarding pair, and it plays nicely with OpenTelemetry.

Trial because running it well has a real operational cost.

name: RabbitMQ
description:
Where I'd reach for a traditional broker with real routing and acknowledgements.

Trialling rather than adopting because I haven't needed it enough to have hard-won opinions.

name: Cloudflare
description:
DNS, Workers, R2 and the rest are fast, cheap and pleasant to use.

Trial because I don't want to depend on a single edge provider for core infrastructure.

name: Kubernetes
description:
Valuable once there are many services and a platform team, but it's a lot of machinery for a small system.

Trial: happy to use it on real work with managed control planes, and I'd avoid running it by hand for one or two services.

name: Railway
description:
Great developer experience for deploying small apps and workers without a platform team.

Trial: excellent for prototypes and side projects, less proven under heavy production load.

name: Go
description:
Where I'd go for small, fast services and CLI tools: quick builds, a single static binary, straightforward concurrency.

Still a trial rather than a default because the type system and dependency ergonomics are a step down from what I'd like.

name: Trunk-based development
description:
Short-lived branches and frequent merges are where I want to be, but it leans on strong CI and feature flags.

Assessing how far I can push it without breaking flow.

name: Rust
description:
Interesting for performance-critical or memory-sensitive pieces, but I haven't shipped anything meaningful in it.

Watching, not committing — the learning cost is real.

name: TDD
description:
I want the safety net, but writing tests first isn't how I actually work and pretending otherwise wastes time. Prefer test-after plus strong types and integration tests.

Revisit for gnarly logic where the design pressure genuinely helps.

name: Service mesh
description:
Too much operational complexity for the workloads I run; most of what I want — mTLS, retries, traffic shaping — is available in the ingress or the platform.

Revisit when there are many heterogeneous services and a team to own it.

name: GCP
description:
Nothing wrong with it, but I don't have the operational familiarity and the ecosystem momentum isn't where I am.

Prefer AWS unless a specific product pulls me in.

name: Vercel
description:
Excellent for Next.js demos, but pricing cliffs and platform lock-in make me cautious for anything with real traffic or a long life.

Prefer deploying the same app somewhere more portable.
